title: Package structure and __init__.py

overview.what:
A package is simply a folder that contains Python files. To tell Python that the folder is a package, you usually place a special file named `__init__.py` inside it.

```python
# A simple file structure:
# my_app/
# ├── __init__.py
# └── calculator.py
```

When you import a package, Python actually runs the code inside `__init__.py` first. This makes `__init__.py` act like a front door to your package.

```python
# Inside my_app/__init__.py
print('The package is being imported!')
VERSION = '1.0'

# In another file, when you import the package:
# import my_app
# Output: The package is being imported!
```

The rule: **`__init__.py` marks a folder as a package and runs automatically upon import.** Think of it like a receptionist at an office. When you enter the building (import the package), the receptionist (`__init__.py`) greets you first.
overview.why: It organizes your code into neat folders, preventing you from putting thousands of lines into one massive file.

why_learning_this: Every real-world project uses folders to separate code.
It helps you avoid ModuleNotFoundError when trying to import your own files.

common_mistakes.title: Putting too much code in __init__.py
common_mistakes.explanation: If you write all your logic inside `__init__.py`, the file gets too large. It should only be used to import things from other files, not to write full functions.

common_mistakes.title: Forgetting __init__.py in older versions
common_mistakes.explanation: While modern Python allows folders without `__init__.py` (called namespace packages), tools often get confused without it. Always include it to be safe.

recall_questions.q: Explain what a package is in your own words, as if to a classmate.
recall_questions.answer: A package is just a folder containing Python files, usually with an __init__.py file inside to tell Python it is a package.

recall_questions.q: What happens automatically when you import a package?
recall_questions.answer: Python runs the code inside the __init__.py file of that package.

recall_questions.q: Why should you avoid putting too much code inside __init__.py?
recall_questions.answer: Because it makes the file too large. It should only act as a front door to import things from other files.

understanding_checks.code:
# Assume my_pkg/__init__.py contains: x = 10
# import my_pkg
# print(my_pkg.x)
print('10')
understanding_checks.question: If you imported `my_pkg` and printed `my_pkg.x`, what would it print?
understanding_checks.why: Importing a package runs its `__init__.py` file, so the variable `x` becomes available directly on the package.

understanding_checks.question: If your folder `my_app` has an empty `__init__.py` file, will Python crash when you `import my_app`?
understanding_checks.why: `__init__.py` can be completely empty. Its mere presence is enough to tell Python that the folder is a package.

code_walkthrough.code:
# Simulate what Python does internally when importing
package_namespace = {}
# Python reads __init__.py and executes it
exec("VERSION = '2.0'", package_namespace)
# Now the package has the variable
print(package_namespace['VERSION'])
